title: What does one order leave you?
principle: Price minus stock cost isn't profit. Count every hidden cost.

screens.text: Let me start with a story. In 2015, an app called PepperTap promised your groceries at home in two hours. By October it handled 20,000 orders a day in 17 cities, and investors had put in more than $50 million. Before I tell you what happened next, have a guess.

screens.prompt: In April 2016, PepperTap shut its grocery delivery. What do you think went wrong?

options.label: A bigger company took its customers

screens.why: It was each order. Thousands of people ordered. But the founder later wrote that they lost more and more money on each order. So more orders meant a bigger loss.

screens.title: The costs that come with each order
screens.text: Now you know what happened. But how can an order lose money when the customer pays? The groceries were only one cost. Each order also had a discount and delivery cost. So let's see what one order really leaves you.

screens.title: What you keep from one order
screens.text: Start with the money from one order. Then remove every cost caused by that order, like stock, delivery, discounts and packing. The money left is called the contribution margin. You still need this money to pay costs like rent and salaries.

screens.prompt: An app sells ₹500 of groceries. After paying the shop, it keeps ₹80. Delivery costs ₹50, and the buyer gets ₹40 off. What's left?
screens.why: Exactly. ₹80 minus ₹50 for delivery and ₹40 for the discount leaves −₹10. So this order loses ₹10. The customer paid ₹500, but you still lost money on the order.

wrong.a: I see what you did: ₹80 is what's left after the shop is paid. But delivery and the discount come out of that same ₹80, and together they cost ₹90, so the order loses ₹10.
wrong.b: You took off delivery, and ₹80 − ₹50 is ₹30. The ₹40 discount comes out of that too, which leaves −₹10, a loss.

screens.prompt: So if every order loses ₹10, what happens when the app doubles its orders?

options.label: The loss gets smaller because the app is bigger

screens.why: Right. At ₹10 lost per order, 20,000 orders lose ₹2 lakh a day, and 40,000 orders lose ₹4 lakh. More losing orders mean a bigger loss. So first make sure each order leaves you some money.

wrong.a: I see why you'd think that, because big businesses often get cheaper costs. But here each order still loses ₹10, so twice the orders means twice the loss.
wrong.c: Nothing changes for a single order: it still loses ₹10. More orders just add up more losses, so the loss doubles.

screens.title: From their story to yours
screens.text: PepperTap's problem can happen in a small business too. A high selling price can make a sale look profitable. But you must count all its costs. Imagine you sell your own T-shirts on Instagram. Let's see what one order leaves you.

screens.prompt: Your ₹499 shirt costs ₹180 to make. Each order also costs ₹70 shipping, ₹15 packing, a ₹10 fee and ₹150 in ads. What's left?
screens.why: Well done. ₹319 minus ₹70, ₹15, ₹10 and ₹150 leaves ₹74. The ads cost almost half of the ₹319 you had left after making the shirt. You would not know this just by looking at the selling price.

wrong.a: I see what you did: you removed shipping, packing and the fee. But you also spent ₹150 on ads to get this buyer. Remove that too, and you are left with ₹74.
wrong.c: That's the price minus the cost of making the shirt. But you must also remove shipping, packing, the fee and ads. After all these costs, you keep ₹74.

screens.prompt: Of 5 orders, 4 arrive and leave you ₹74 each. 1 buyer refuses the parcel, and that costs you ₹305. What do all 5 leave?
screens.why: That's it. The four delivered orders leave 4 × ₹74 = ₹296. The refused order costs ₹305. So the five orders together leave −₹9. This is why many sellers ask buyers to pay before delivery.

wrong.b: You counted the four delivered orders correctly: they leave ₹296. But the refused parcel didn't just earn nothing; it cost ₹305, so the five orders together leave −₹9.
wrong.c: I see what you did: 5 × ₹74. But only four orders were delivered, and they leave ₹296, while the refused parcel cost ₹305. Together, that's −₹9.

screens.prompt: Imagine you have a magic wand. You can make one cost 20% cheaper: the ₹180 shirt, ₹150 ads or ₹70 shipping. Which do you pick?
screens.why: Yes, the shirt. 20% of ₹180 is ₹36, more than the ads (₹30) or shipping (₹14). In real life, start with your biggest cost. Ask your shirt maker for a lower price before trying to reduce shipping.

wrong.b: Close. Ads are a big cost too. But 20% of ₹150 is ₹30, while 20% of the ₹180 shirt is ₹36. Cutting 20% from the bigger cost saves more money.
wrong.c: You may choose shipping because you see that bill often. But 20% of ₹70 is only ₹14. Cutting 20% from the ₹180 shirt saves ₹36.

screens.prompt: Your plain shirt leaves ₹74 and sells 15 a week. A printed one leaves ₹130 and sells 10. Which earns you more each week?

options.label: The plain one, because it sells more

screens.why: Well done. The plain shirt earns 15 × ₹74 = ₹1,110 a week. The printed one earns 10 × ₹130 = ₹1,300. Selling more shirts does not always mean earning more money. Count the money each product leaves per week.

wrong.a: I see why: selling more shirts can look better. But 15 × ₹74 is ₹1,110, while 10 × ₹130 is ₹1,300. So the printed shirt earns more.
wrong.b: Work out each one: 15 × ₹74 = ₹1,110 and 10 × ₹130 = ₹1,300. The printed shirt earns ₹190 more a week.

screens.setup: Then a shop owner from Surat calls. She wants 100 of your shirts a month at ₹350 each. She'll collect them herself, so there's no shipping, no ads and no refused parcels, and you'd only pack them, at ₹15 a shirt.
screens.question: ₹350 is much less than your ₹499 price. Should you take this order?

options.label: Say no. I'd lose ₹149 a shirt
options.outcome: She buys from another maker. You keep selling online at ₹499, where one delivered order leaves you ₹74. Her order would have left you ₹15,500 a month, but you lose that order.
options.why: You compared the two selling prices. But you should compare what each sale leaves you. ₹350 − ₹180 − ₹15 = ₹155. That is more than double the ₹74 an online order leaves.
options.better: Work out what each shirt leaves before you say no.

options.label: Say yes. With no shipping or ads, it pays
options.outcome: ₹350 minus the ₹180 shirt and ₹15 packing leaves ₹155 a shirt, more than double the ₹74 an online order leaves. You say yes, and 100 shirts leave you ₹15,500 a month.
options.why: Well done. A lower selling price can leave you more money when that sale has fewer costs.

options.label: Say yes only if she pays ₹499
options.outcome: She says no and stops replying. A week later you agree to ₹350 after all, but she has already given half the order to another maker, so 50 shirts leave you ₹7,750 a month.
options.why: You asked for a higher price even though ₹350 already left you a good amount. Because of that, you lost half the order.
options.better: First work out what each sale leaves you. Then you will know if the price is good.

screens.text: Price minus stock cost is not profit. What one ___ leaves after every cost it causes is its contribution ___.
screens.why: Exactly. PepperTap had 20,000 orders a day. But more orders cannot fix an order that loses money. The money each sale leaves helps pay rent and wages. So before you try to get more sales, check that each sale leaves you some money.

summary: Contribution margin is what one order leaves after every cost it causes.
Ads, delivery, discounts and refused parcels can turn a 'good' sale into a loss.
A fast seller can earn less than a slow one. Count rupees per week.

cards.front: Price ₹600, stock ₹300, delivery ₹80, ads ₹200. What's the contribution margin per order?
cards.back: ₹600 − ₹300 − ₹80 − ₹200 = ₹20. Every cost an order causes comes off.

cards.front: Item A leaves ₹5 and sells 100 a day. Item B leaves ₹12 and sells 50. Which earns more a day?
cards.back: B: ₹600 a day. A: ₹500. Count rupees, not units.
